blocks.text: “Hey! Hey!” said the old man as he came to the door. “Do you have anything to sell?”

We naturally stepped back and looked quickly at the woman who had led us there. She had taken a key from her pocket and had been trying to open the house door with it. Richard spoke to her now. He said we had had the pleasure of seeing where she lived, and we were short of time. So we would leave her now. But it was not so easy to leave her. In a strange and urgent way, she begged us very seriously to walk upstairs and see her room for just a moment. In her harmless way, she was also very determined to lead me inside, as part of the sign of good luck that she wanted. I saw that, whatever the others might do, there was nothing I could do except agree. I suppose we were all more or less curious. In any case, the old man joined her in trying to persuade us. “Yes, yes! Please her!” he said. “It won't take a minute! Come in, come in! Come in through the shop, if the other door is out of order!” When he said this, we all went inside. Richard laughed and encouraged us, making us more eager to go, and we trusted him to protect us.

“My landlord, Krook,” said the little old lady as she introduced him to us. From her grand, high position, she treated him with the polite kindness shown to someone lower in rank. “The neighbours call him the Lord Chancellor. His shop is called the Court of Chancery. He is a very unusual person in his ways. He is very odd. Oh, I can tell you for certain, he is very odd!”

She shook her head a great many times and tapped her forehead with her finger. By doing this, she wanted to show us that we must be kind enough to excuse him. “Because he is a little—you know!—M—!” said the old lady, in a very grand and formal way. The old man heard what she said to us, and he laughed.

He walked in front of us with the lantern. “It's true enough that they call me the Lord Chancellor, and call my shop Chancery,” he said. “And why do you think they call me the Lord Chancellor, and my shop Chancery?”
“I really don't know!” said Richard, not caring very much.

The old man stopped and turned round. “You see,” he said, “they— Hey! Here's lovely hair! I have got three large bags of ladies' hair downstairs, but none of it is as beautiful and fine as this. What color, and what a wonderful feel it has!”

“That is enough, my good friend!” said Richard. The old man had slid one long piece of Ada's hair through his yellow hand, and Richard strongly disapproved of this. “You can admire, as the rest of us do, without doing something you have no right to do.”

The old man threw a sudden, quick look at him. That look even pulled my attention away from Ada. Ada had been suddenly surprised, and a red color had risen in her cheeks. She was so unusually beautiful that she seemed to hold steady the wandering attention of the little old lady herself. But then Ada spoke up between them. Laughing, she said that she could only feel proud of such real, honest admiration. As she said this, Mr. Krook shrank back into his earlier self, just as suddenly as he had jumped out of it.

He held up the lantern and began speaking again. “You see, I have so many things here, of so many different kinds,” he said. “The neighbours think that all of them are slowly wasting away and falling into complete ruin—though they know nothing! That is why they have given those names to me and my place. And among my goods, I have so many old parchments—sheets of animal skin used for writing—and so many old papers. And I like rust, damp mould, and spiderwebs. And everything that comes my way is a good catch to me, like anything caught in a fisherman's net. And I cannot stand to give up anything once I get hold of it—or so my neighbours think, though what do they know? I also cannot stand to change anything, or to have any sweeping, scrubbing, cleaning, or repairing happening around me. That is how I have got the bad name of Chancery. I don't mind. Almost every day, I go to see my noble and highly educated brother, when he sits as judge in the Inn. He doesn't notice me, but I notice him. There is no great difference between us. We both keep digging away in a confused mess. Hey, Lady Jane!”
